content: Clinicians have employed various surgical techniques to reduce the likelihood of recurrent prolapse following traditional native tissue repair, such as anterior colporrhaphy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of surgical interventions for anterior compartment prolapse. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and MEDLINE, as well as handsearched journals, conference proceedings, and trial registries. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated surgical procedures for anterior compartment prolapse. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for bias, extracted data, and analyzed the results. The primary outcomes assessed were patient awareness of prolapse, the need for repeat surgery, and recurrent prolapse as determined by clinical examination. A total of 33 trials involving 3,332 women were included in the analysis. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations due to bias and imprecision. The findings for the main comparisons are as follows: Native Tissue Repair vs. Biological Graft Awareness of Prolapse: There was little to no difference between the two groups (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.82; low-quality evidence). If 12% of women were aware of prolapse after biological graft repair, 7% to 23% would be aware after native tissue repair. Repeat Surgery for Prolapse: No significant difference was observed between the groups (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.97; moderate-quality evidence). If 4% of women required repeat surgery after biological graft repair, 2% to 9% would require it after native tissue repair. Recurrent Anterior Compartment Prolapse: Native tissue repair likely increased the risk of recurrence (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.65; moderate-quality evidence). If 26% of women experienced recurrence after biological graft repair, 27% to 42% would experience recurrence after native tissue repair. Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI): No significant difference was found between the groups (RR 1.44, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.64; moderate-quality evidence). Dyspareunia: There was little to no difference between the groups (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.93; low-quality evidence). Native Tissue Repair vs. Polypropylene Mesh Awareness of Prolapse: Awareness of prolapse was more likely after native tissue repair (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.28; moderate-quality evidence). If 13% of women were aware of prolapse after mesh repair, 18% to 30% would be aware after native tissue repair. Repeat Surgery for Prolapse: Repeat surgery was more likely after native tissue repair (RR 2.03, 95% CI 1.15 to 3.58; moderate-quality evidence). If 2% of women required repeat surgery after mesh repair, 2% to 7% would require it after native tissue repair. Recurrent Anterior Compartment Prolapse: Recurrence was more likely after native tissue repair (RR 3.01, 95% CI 2.52 to 3.60; moderate-quality evidence). If 13% of women experienced recurrence after mesh repair, 32% to 45% would experience recurrence after native tissue repair. Composite Outcome (Repeat Surgery for Prolapse, SUI, or Mesh Exposure): This was less likely after native tissue repair (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.83; moderate-quality evidence). If 10% of women required repeat surgery after polypropylene mesh repair, 4% to 8% would require it after native tissue repair. De Novo SUI: There was little to no difference between the groups (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.01; low-quality evidence). No significant difference was observed in rates of repeat surgery for SUI. Dyspareunia (De Novo): There was little to no difference between the groups (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.27 to 1.06; low-quality evidence). Native Tissue Repair vs. Absorbable Mesh Awareness of Prolapse: It is unclear whether there were differences between the groups (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.31; very low-quality evidence). Repeat Surgery for Prolapse: It is unclear whether there were differences between the groups (RR 2.13, 95% CI 0.42 to 10.82; very low-quality evidence). Recurrent Anterior Compartment Prolapse: Recurrence was more likely after native tissue repair (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.06; moderate-quality evidence). If 27% of women experienced recurrence after mesh repair, 29% to 55% would experience recurrence after native tissue repair. SUI: It is unclear whether there were differences between the groups (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.05; very low-quality evidence). Dyspareunia: No data were reported. Authors' Conclusions Biological graft repair or absorbable mesh offers minimal advantage over native tissue repair. Native tissue repair was associated with increased awareness of prolapse, higher rates of repeat surgery for prolapse, and greater risk of recurrent anterior compartment prolapse compared to polypropylene mesh repair. However, native tissue repair was associated with a reduced risk of de novo SUI, fewer bladder injuries, and lower rates of repeat surgery for prolapse, SUI, and mesh exposure (composite outcome). Current evidence does not support the routine use of mesh repair over native tissue repair for anterior compartment prolapse due to increased morbidity. Many transvaginal polypropylene meshes have been voluntarily withdrawn from the market, and newer lightweight transvaginal meshes have not been evaluated in RCTs. Clinicians and patients should exercise caution when considering these products, as their safety and efficacy remain unproven.
